short: A request from a program to the kernel: the only way user-space code can read a file, send a packet or ask for memory.
The core of the operating system: it owns the hardware, the memory, the files and the network stack, and runs with full CPU privileges.
Two worlds enforced by the CPU: your program lives in user space and can only compute; the kernel lives in kernel space and can touch everything.
A small non-negative integer a process uses to refer to something it has opened: a file, a socket, a pipe, a terminal. It is an index into the process's own table in the kernel.
The kernel object created by one open: it holds the offset and the flags. A file descriptor points to it; dup and fork make several descriptors point to the same one.
The error code a failed syscall reports: -1 plus a number with a name such as ENOENT (no such file) or EAGAIN (try again later).
What a reader sees when no more data will ever come. For a file: the end. For a TCP connection: the peer closed (or shut down) its sending side. read returns 0.
A kernel object that is one end of a communication channel, reached through a file descriptor. For TCP: one end of a connection (or a listening end that accepts connections).
The reliable, ordered byte-stream protocol on top of IP: it sets up a connection (3-way handshake), numbers bytes, retransmits losses and controls the sending rate.
A 16-bit number that tells the kernel which socket on a machine should receive a packet. Ports below 1024 need privileges to listen on.
A tool that prints every syscall a program makes, with its arguments and result. The main window into the kernel's front door.
A syscall that copies bytes from one file descriptor to another entirely inside the kernel, so the data never enters your program's memory.
A fixed-size fingerprint of a file's bytes. Equal fingerprints mean equal bytes, for all practical purposes.
Go interfaces for "something you can read bytes from" and "something you can write bytes to". Files, connections, pipes and standard input/output all implement them.
The position in an open file where the next read or write starts. It is stored in the open file description, not in the file and not in the descriptor.
The kernel's copy of file contents in memory, in 4 KB pages. Reads are served from it; writes go into it first (dirty pages) and reach the disk later.
A Linux interface to wait for many descriptors at once: register them with epoll_ctl, then epoll_wait returns the ones that are ready.
The second argument of listen: how many finished connections the kernel keeps in the accept queue, waiting for the program to call accept.
The state the side that closes a TCP connection first stays in for 60 seconds, so that late segments of the old connection cannot be mistaken for a new one.
How many more bytes a TCP receiver can take right now: the free room in its receive buffer, sent in every segment. A sender never sends beyond it.
A TCP rule (RFC 896): a segment smaller than the maximum size waits while earlier data is unacknowledged, so many small writes travel as a few segments. TCP_NODELAY turns it off.
How long TCP waits for an acknowledgement before sending a segment again; computed from the measured round-trip time, at least 200 ms on Linux, doubled after each timeout.
A descriptor with O_NONBLOCK: a call that would have to wait fails at once with EAGAIN instead.
The kernel's object for a socket: state, addresses, send and receive buffers, sequence numbers, timers. ss -tnoemi prints much of it.
